Suez Canal. An artificial waterway that links the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea by running through Egypt, eliminating the need for ships to navigate all the way around Africa. Opened in eighteen sixty-nine, it became one of the world's most strategically vital shipping routes.

The canal spans roughly one hundred and ninety-three kilometers through the Sinai Peninsula and Egyptian territory, connecting Port Said on the Mediterranean to Port Suez on the Red Sea. It was conceived and directed by Ferdinand de Lesseps, a French diplomat and engineer who oversaw its construction from eighteen fifty-nine to eighteen sixty-nine using predominantly Egyptian labor. The project cost enormous resources and Egyptian lives.

The canal shortened shipping routes from Europe to Asia dramatically, reducing transit times from months circling Africa to just days. This shifted global trade patterns profoundly. Britain quickly secured financial control and eventual political dominance of the canal following its construction, positioning itself as guardian of the route and guarantor of access. This strategic dominance underpinned British naval supremacy for decades.

In nineteen fifty-six, Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized the canal in response to Western pressure, sparking what became known as the Suez Crisis. Britain, France, and Israel invaded militarily but were forced to withdraw by pressure from the United States and the Soviet Union. Egypt has controlled the canal since then.

Today it remains one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, handling roughly thirteen thousand vessels annually and approximately thirty percent of global containerized cargo. Traffic has increased dramatically since Egypt took control, and the canal is now a crucial source of revenue and strategic leverage for Egypt in regional politics. Even temporary closures, like the grounding of the Ever Given in twenty twenty-one, have worldwide economic impact.
